title: Year four close
hookLine: a year with thinkers and schools

lines: THE WOODS. SOLID AND LIGHT. THANK YOU.
cards: Like water. My attempt. Look as if for the first time.
Go to the woods. Solid and light. Thank you.
Those lines closed each stretch of this year: the Tao Te Ching, Montaigne, Emerson, Thoreau, the science, and the tour of the world's schools.
Read in a row, they sound less like conclusions and more like directions for a walk. Soften. Try.

teach.b: First, four companions, read slowly. Lao Tzu, whose book begins by admitting that words fall short. Montaigne, who wrote about himself in pieces he called attempts.
Emerson, who asked readers to look as if for the first time. Thoreau, who went to live by a pond to see what life had to teach. None of them asked to be obeyed.
Each walked beside you for a while, then let you go.
Second, science, told honestly. Attention, habit and compassion can grow, the studies said, modestly. So the year's rule was simple: keep what's solid, hold the rest lightly.
Third, the world's schools, never ranked: Zen halls and Sufi circles, Jewish study pairs and Quaker silence, Hindu chant and Sikh dawn prayer, Chinese parks at sunrise, each met in its own words.
This last week asked what drew you, what doesn't fit, and what you actually do.
Fourth, water, one more time. The Tao Te Ching, in its eighth chapter, says the highest good is like water. Water benefits everything and doesn't contend.
It settles in the low places people look down on. Elsewhere the book adds that nothing is softer than water, yet nothing does better against what is hard.

Watch any stream: the water doesn't fight the stone; it goes around. The year's first book gives a fair picture of how to walk out of it: not racing to the top, not standing still, but moving on, steadily and low.

how: Some people close a year of study with a slow walk, recalling what they read and choosing one line to carry into the next year; some traditions keep a walking meditation of their own.

games.why: today's lesson, from the Tao Te Ching's water: not racing, not standing still, but moving on, steadily and low.

practice: If you can stand and move, walk a room or a hallway at half your usual speed, letting your path bend around what's there, a chair, a doorframe, a corner, without pushing anything aside, and letting each step settle before the next.
If walking isn't possible, let your breath move like water instead, never forced, or trace a slow, winding path with one hand. Nowhere to arrive; if you pray, you can walk with a prayer.

wordCard.voice: Year four close. A year with thinkers and schools: four companions read slowly, science told honestly, and the world's ways of practice, each in its own words. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese dao, the way: the word the Tao Te Ching opens with, and the book this year began with.
